description: Machine-readable registry of M13 audit findings and observations for the SAR Rust reference implementation. Covers parser, memory, panic, DoS, fuzzing, and documentation findings and observations from the M13a.1 audit, cryptography and secret-handling findings and observations from the M13a.2 audit, transform and recovery resource-accounting findings and observations from the M13a.3 audit, filesystem metadata and extraction safety findings and observations from the M13a.4 audit, crate-boundary, profile-boundary, transport, and FFI-readiness findings and observations from the M13a.5 audit, and cold-storage and tape-resilience findings and observations from the M13a.6 audit.

objectives.title: Audit cryptographic dependency usage
objectives.summary: Workspace and crate cryptographic dependencies, feature selection, algorithm dispatch, and safe API usage were reviewed. The audited paths use a narrow dependency set, safe high-level AEAD APIs, and fail-closed dispatch for unsupported non-AEAD modes.

objectives.title: Audit authentication failure behavior
objectives.summary: Archive and transport authentication failures were traced through success and failure paths. The audited implementations fail closed, reject post-binding plaintext in TLS_EXPORTER sessions, and avoid releasing plaintext before authentication succeeds.

objectives.title: Audit TLS_EXPORTER SAR-AEAD key derivation
objectives.summary: TLS_EXPORTER KMS parsing, context encoding, transport exporter integration, and negative-path evidence were reviewed. Unsupported AEAD and Global Header hash IDs and mismatched derived-key lengths are accepted by parsing and remain unvalidated by in-repo consumers, so unsupported or inconsistent TLS_EXPORTER parameters are not guaranteed to fail closed end-to-end.

objectives.title: Audit AAD binding behavior
objectives.summary: AAD construction across archive, selective-FEC, and additional QUIC control-stream paths was reviewed. Current selective-FEC and transport controls were verified, and the previously recorded unchecked Global Flags length narrowing in AAD construction remains relevant to this objective.

objectives.title: Audit AEAD tag failure behavior
objectives.summary: AEAD tag parsing and failure behavior were reviewed across archive and transport call paths. Tag failures are treated as hard errors for the authenticated unit and do not permit continued processing of unauthenticated plaintext.

objectives.title: Audit constant-time handling of secret comparisons where comparison is unavoidable
objectives.summary: Secret-dependent comparisons in the audited scope were reviewed. Digest equality uses a constant-time helper, and AEAD tag verification remains inside vetted crypto library operations rather than open-coded byte comparisons.

objectives.title: Audit zeroization of exporter-derived material where practical
objectives.summary: Zeroization practicality was reviewed for CEKs, derived keys, password material, and failure buffers. The audited crypto paths consistently wrap secret material in zeroizing containers and explicitly clear plaintext buffers on authentication failure.

objectives.title: Audit logs, errors, debug APIs, and test helpers for accidental secret exposure
objectives.summary: Errors, debug exposure surfaces, CLI secret-entry paths, precedence, and user-facing guidance were reviewed. A safer interactive password path already exists, but current CLI help and documentation do not clearly warn against argv/environment exposure channels or consistently prefer the safer path.

objectives.title: Audit decompressor setup limits and decoded output bounds
objectives.summary: Decompressor decoded output is bounded by max_output_size via copy_bounded before any decompressed byte reaches the caller; algorithm IDs are validated before decoder construction; and the STORE, DEFLATE, and ZSTD paths all route through the same bounded copy path. SAR documentation does not currently state that decoder library-internal working memory is outside the documented ResourceLimits surface; that documentation gap is recorded in M13-TRANSFORM-008.

objectives.title: Audit patch and delta setup limits
objectives.summary: BSDIFF and VCDIFF limits (patch size, block counts, output size) are correctly derived from unified ResourceLimits via adapter functions before patch application. However, the complete fuzz target inventory does not meaningfully reach BSDIFF or VCDIFF patch application with attacker-controlled base-plus-patch inputs, and no fuzz target reaches the archive-level repair APIs; that narrowed gap is recorded in M13-TRANSFORM-007.

objectives.title: Audit algorithm-switching and profile-based algorithm restrictions
objectives.summary: SAR archives use per-entry algorithm IDs read from each LFH; unsupported or reserved IDs fail closed at decode time with no per-session algorithm-switching state to exploit. However, the specification does not define per-profile normative algorithm restriction tables, leaving implementors without a basis to enforce profile-specific algorithm constraints before entry processing. No unsafe code was found in any audited transform or recovery crate.

objectives.title: Audit delta target-size and output-size invariants
objectives.summary: Declared target size (LFH Uncompressed Size) is verified after patch application for all implemented algorithms. STORE_PATCH, BSDIFF, and VCDIFF all return PatchFailed when reconstructed output length does not equal the declared size. Arithmetic throughout the BSDIFF and VCDIFF implementations uses checked operations.

objectives.title: Audit sparse reconstruction limits
objectives.summary: Sparse reconstruction allocates exactly logical_size bytes, bounded before allocation by max_decoded_entry_size and max_allocation_bytes. Extent validation uses checked arithmetic, enforces non-overlapping ascending-offset order, and rejects zero-length extents, out-of-bounds extents, and excess payload bytes. Fragment group validation enforces count, group span, and loss-tolerant gap limits before reassembly.

objectives.title: Audit FEC and recovery metadata bounds
objectives.summary: FEC value byte length is bounded by check_fec_value_bytes before codec construction in both LFH and recovery TLV paths. XOR and RS codecs independently enforce a 256 MiB MAX_PARITY_SIZE constant on parity allocation. Stripe, group, and parity products use checked arithmetic throughout. Recovery TLV IDs outside the defined range are rejected before value parsing.

objectives.title: Audit in-memory recovery API limitations
objectives.summary: The `repair_archive` API is explicitly documented as an in-memory API and applies `max_archive_size`, `max_recovery_protected_range`, and a partial `max_repair_working_set` check before repair execution. Tracing source-visible ownership at `Vec::with_capacity(archive_bytes.len())` (during repaired-output allocation in `repair_archive()`): `layout.recovery_tlvs` (`R` bytes) and `erasure_indices` (`E` bytes) remain in scope and allocated alongside the caller-owned archive slice (`X`), the recovered protected-range output (`P`), and the repaired full-archive output being allocated (`X`). The minimum proven repaired-output peak is `2X + P`; the full source-visible peak is at least `2X + P + R + E`. The checked formula `X + 2P + T` does not match the source-visible repaired-output lifetime set: it omits the repaired output `X`, omits most of `R` and all of `E`, and includes a second `protected_range.length` term that has no corresponding source-visible live allocation at that peak; the total simultaneous retained memory is therefore undercounted.

objectives.title: Audit profile-specific strict-mode rejection behavior
objectives.summary: validate_archive_profile checks global-flag constraints per profile. Per-entry algorithm ID validation is documented as a known limitation not yet implemented. The specification requires returning SAR_ERR_UNSUPPORTED for algorithm IDs not supported by the selected profile but does not provide per-profile normative algorithm restriction tables; this specification gap is recorded.

objectives.title: Audit archive path validation and normalization behavior
objectives.summary: Archive entry names and symlink parent components are lexically validated before joining to the output tree; absolute, UNC, drive-prefixed, empty, dot, and dot-dot components are rejected, and existing symlink parents are refused.
notes: M13b.3 Package F: historical outcome preserved. Path classification now reports SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE for escapes; see M13-EXTRACT-002.

objectives.title: Audit output-root confinement and replacement-race behavior
objectives.summary: The extractor performs lexical checks but does not canonicalize or hold directory-relative handles for final create, rename, or metadata operations, so output-root symlinks and concurrent path replacement remain security-relevant.
notes: M13b.3 Package F: the path-based mutation model recorded here was replaced on Unix by descriptor-relative operations (Packages A-E); non-Unix extraction is refused. The finding M13-EXTRACT-001 stays confirmed pending acceptance of the platform limitations recorded there.

objectives.title: Audit symlink target semantics and hardlink handling
objectives.summary: Hardlink creation is absent from the current entry model and extractor, and symlink extraction stays opt-in, but the specification does not yet resolve whether escaping or absolute symlink targets are conforming archive content or must be rejected for extraction safety.
notes: M13b.3 Package F: the symlink-target normative question was resolved (M13a.7) and implemented for ordinary extraction in Package B; still no hardlink Entry kind.

objectives.title: Audit permission restoration and directory staging/finalization ordering
objectives.summary: New directories are staged with a chmod to mode 0o700 that succeeds before any archive content is written (failing closed on error); directory metadata is finalized after child extraction in reverse-depth order; and restored permission modes are masked to ordinary permission bits. The initial creation via `fs::create_dir()` uses the process umask, so the directory exists briefly at a umask-determined mode before the chmod; during that window the directory is empty and other local principals with parent-directory access can observe its existence but cannot write to it under ordinary mode-bit semantics.
notes: M13b.3 Package F: the umask-dependent create-then-chmod window no longer exists on Unix (directories are created 0700 descriptor-relative).

objectives.title: Audit owner and timestamp restoration hazards
objectives.summary: Owner and timestamp restoration are opt-in and symlink metadata application is skipped, but the underlying path-based metadata calls inherit the unresolved confinement and race issue tracked separately.
notes: M13b.3 Package F: owner, timestamp and permission restoration are applied to open descriptors and never re-resolve paths on Unix; still opt-in.

objectives.title: Audit platform-specific extraction safety branches
objectives.summary: Non-Unix builds fail closed when symlink extraction or owner or permission restoration is requested, so the Unix-only mutation paths remain the platform-specific extraction surface reviewed here.
notes: M13b.3 Package F: non-Unix targets now refuse all extraction instead of only unsupported restoration requests; macOS runtime remains unverified.

objectives.title: Crate-boundary attack surface
objectives.summary: The primary crate-boundary risk identified is that `TransportConfig` propagates only `max_active_streams` into the `ResourceLimits` used by `StreamArchiveParser` and `SessionManager` inside `InMemoryTransport`, leaving all other limits at their defaults. This fixed-default boundary contract is undocumented at the transport API boundary. The reviewed crate roots for `sar-transport`, `sar-stream`, `sar-archive`, `sar-compression`, `sar-delta`, `sar-fec`, `sar-fragmentation`, `sar-loss-tolerant`, `sar-sparse`, `sar-crypto`, and `sar-core` all carry `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. No reviewed cross-crate ownership, aliasing, or lifetime assumption risks were found beyond the documented `KeyProvider` trait-object callback model addressed in FFI objectives.

objectives.title: Profile and library-layout attack surface
objectives.summary: `validate_archive_profile` is explicitly documented as global-header-only and does not enforce entry-level algorithm restrictions, per-entry LOSS_TOLERANT presence, or unsafe path rejection. The reviewed public `sar-archive` profile API surface is limited to `ComplianceProfile`, `ProfileReport`, `validate_archive_profile`, and profile name conversion helpers; no reviewed public entry-iterating profile-validation entry point was identified. The `Standard` profile variant is a placeholder. The normative algorithm restriction tables that would back per-entry algorithm enforcement remain unresolved and are tracked in M13-TRANSFORM-001. Profile state is not carried through the transport or session layer; callers must apply profile validation separately. No additional profile-bypass paths or unsafe component compositions were identified in the reviewed profile, transport, and session artifacts.

objectives.title: Transport and session attack surface
objectives.summary: The transport inactivity watchdog is caller-opt-in and the activation requirement is not documented at the `TransportConfig` level. `QuicSarConnection::feed_stream_bytes` requires a follow-up `flush_pending_control_frames` call to emit outbound control frames, but this ordering requirement is absent from the public method docstring. Both are documentation gaps. A positive control was confirmed: `InMemoryTransport` enforces fail-closed behavior for TLS_EXPORTER-bound sessions at the transport parsing layer, rejecting unencrypted entries before any downstream processing. TLS_EXPORTER KMS parameter validation and AEAD fail-closed behavior are tracked in M13-CRYPTO-001 and M13-CRYPTO-004 respectively and are not duplicated here.

objectives.title: FFI-readiness risks
objectives.summary: Three FFI-readiness gaps were identified: (1) the `KeyProvider` trait callback model requires a purpose-built stable wrapper for any foreign binding because it uses Rust-specific trait objects, `Send + Sync` bounds, and zeroizing secret containers; (2) `SarError::Io(std::io::Error)` is not ABI-stable and must be mapped to `SarStatus` codes before crossing a language boundary; (3) the listed QUIC connection and stream I/O APIs are `async fn` and require an async runtime or event-loop adapter for synchronous C or Python wrappers, while the synchronous TCP API (`TcpSarConnection`) is more amenable to blocking wrappers. None of these is a security finding; all are documentation gaps requiring remediation in M13b.4.

objectives.title: Public Rust APIs exposing unstable layout, ownership, or lifetime assumptions
objectives.summary: Across the reviewed source artifacts and public API inventory entries, no reviewed API was found to rely on stable foreign-compatible memory layout, stable Rust discriminants, unsafe aliasing, or unsound lifetime assumptions. The reviewed public surfaces include ordinary safe Rust ownership forms, borrowed references, `&'static str`, trait objects, and generic I/O, but those forms are not presented as stable FFI representations. No `repr(C)`, `transmute`, `from_raw`, `into_raw`, `offset_of`, `size_of`, or `align_of` usage was found in the reviewed source artifacts. The absence of layout-stability claims is consistent with the API inventory's `readiness: candidate` status for most types.

objectives.title: APIs that should remain Rust-only
objectives.summary: The existing `SecretBytes` and `SecretString` Rust types (sar-crypto) should remain Rust-only because their zeroizing ownership and destruction semantics must not become part of a foreign ABI. A purpose-built wrapper may copy key material through an explicitly owned and zeroized boundary representation without exposing these concrete types. `BinaryWriter` and `ParseCursor` (sar-core) are internal parsing and writing helpers not intended as stable surface; they are marked `candidate: false` in the API inventory. `StreamArchiveParser`, `StreamWriteState`, `StreamStep`, `StreamEvent`, and `StreamArchiveSummary` (sar-archive) are marked `not_ready` in the inventory and depend on `Box<dyn KeyProvider>` and generic I/O that require purpose-built wrappers before any foreign exposure. No additional Rust-only classification beyond the API inventory's existing recommendations was required.

objectives.title: APIs potentially suitable for future C or Python wrappers
objectives.summary: Plausible wrapper candidates with ordinary conversion include: `SarStatus` (ready integer enum), `GlobalFlags` (uint32 bitmask), simple metadata structs (`EntryKind`, `EntryPermissionMetadata`, `EntryTimestampMetadata`, `EntryCompressionMetadata`), `ResourceLimits` (flat config struct), `CompressionAlgorithm`, and `validate_archive_profile` paired with `ComplianceProfile`. Candidates requiring a purpose-built stable wrapper include: `ArchiveReader`/`ArchiveWriter` (generic I/O; need opaque handles and owned-buffer operations), `SessionManager` (complex state machine; suitable only through explicit create/step/destroy lifecycle), `KeyProvider` (blocked by M13-FFI-001), and QUIC APIs (blocked by M13-FFI-003). `SarError` requires the `SarStatus` mapping described in M13-FFI-002 before use in any wrapper. APIs that should remain Rust-only for concrete reasons are classified in OBJ-06.

objectives.title: Structural-anchor recoverability matrix for plain SAR v1.0
objectives.summary: The recoverability of all required structural anchor classes was assessed against the reviewed specification and source artifacts. Global Header byte-0-7 loss and CD/Footer loss are accepted design risks (COLD-001, COLD-002) because both regions are outside the RECOVERY TLV protected range. Entry-header and payload corruption within the protected range is detectable and, when erasure positions are known, recoverable via FEC. Isolated payload corruption without AEAD or hash protection is detectable only if a DATA_HASH or AEAD tag is present; without such protection it may be undetectable. Fragmentation metadata loss (Fragment ID, Fragment Index) prevents complete reassembly and is not reconstructable by plain SAR v1.0 FEC. LOSS_TOLERANT processing (Section 6.2.2 and 19.4.5) permits best-effort entry continuation for temporal data but does not restore structural anchors or missing fragment metadata. Truncation after complete entries but before terminal metadata (CD and Footer) may leave Data Area bytes structurally salvageable, but normal indexed parsing and archive repair cannot reconstruct the CD/Footer or access RECOVERY metadata after terminal-anchor loss. A dedicated implementation-defined sequential salvage path may recover some entries; Section 19.4.4 defines degraded recovery specifically for `PARTITIONED_ARCHIVE` and does not establish general complete-archive reconstruction. Multiple disjoint unreadable regions require that erasure positions be known before RECOVERY decoding; if positions cannot be determined, SAR_ERR_RECOVERY_UNAVAILABLE applies per Section 9.2. FEC-protected payload recovery within an LFH scope (SELECTIVE_FEC) is bounded by RECOVERY-002. In-memory recovery API limitations are documented in RECOVERY-003.

objectives.title: Global Header loss and corruption recoverability
objectives.summary: Archive bytes 0-7 (Magic Number through Flags Size) are outside the RECOVERY TLV protected range per Section 9.2. Missing bytes, or corruption that produces an invalid Magic Number, Version, Reserved value, or Flags Size, cause `parse_global_header()` to fail before the protected range can be consulted. Corruption that remains syntactically valid may not be detected by Global Header parsing, and plain SAR v1.0 cannot reconstruct the original bytes 0-7 in either case. The accepted design risk is recorded as COLD-001.

objectives.title: Central Dictionary and Footer loss and corruption recoverability
objectives.summary: The Central Dictionary and Footer are explicitly outside the RECOVERY TLV protected range per Section 9.2. RECOVERY parity data resides inside the CD; loss or total corruption of the CD simultaneously removes the parity required for protected-range repair. `parse_archive_layout()` returns `cd_offset: None` only for `NO_INDEX` archives; when the Footer or CD cannot be parsed it returns an error before RECOVERY metadata becomes available. Data Area bytes may remain structurally salvageable, but normal indexed parsing and archive repair cannot reconstruct or access RECOVERY metadata after terminal-anchor loss. A dedicated implementation-defined sequential salvage path may recover some entries; Section 19.4.4 defines degraded recovery specifically for `PARTITIONED_ARCHIVE` and does not constitute general complete-archive reconstruction. The accepted design risk is recorded as COLD-002.

objectives.title: Entry-header, payload, fragmentation metadata, and FEC metadata recoverability
objectives.summary: Entry-header and payload bytes within the RECOVERY TLV protected range are recoverable when erasure positions are known and parity data is intact in the CD. Isolated payload corruption is detectable via AEAD authentication or DATA_HASH, and is recoverable via FEC if in-scope and erasure-position determinable. FEC value byte length and parity allocation are bounded before codec construction (RECOVERY-002). LOSS_TOLERANT (Section 6.2.2 and 19.4.5) permits best-effort fragment continuation but does not reconstruct missing structural metadata. Fragment ID and Fragment Index loss prevents correct reassembly; LOSS_TOLERANT fills missing fragment positions with null bytes or unwritten regions but does not restore lost index values. The in-memory recovery API documents its limitations and partial working-set bounds (RECOVERY-003); the repaired-output peak accounting gap is tracked in RECOVERY-001.

objectives.title: Sidecar recovery index approach evaluation
objectives.summary: A SAR-specific external recovery sidecar is an external artifact produced alongside the SAR archive containing enough recovery metadata to reconstruct a lost or corrupted CD or Footer. The approach leaves the original SAR byte stream unchanged; a specification-compliant SAR reader that receives only the original archive file can read it directly without the sidecar. Recovering from CD/Footer loss requires locating, binding, and validating the sidecar before opening the archive. The recovered archive, once repaired, is an ordinary SAR v1.0 archive. SAR v1.0 defines no normative SAR-specific sidecar format or archive-binding mechanism; the approach requires further normative definition to be interoperable. The specification gap is recorded as SPEC-002.

objectives.title: External parity and recovery container approach evaluation
objectives.summary: An external parity or recovery container (for example a separate erasure-coded copy of the full archive byte stream) leaves the original SAR byte stream unchanged. An unaware SAR reader can read the original archive directly without the container. Recovery from the external container requires decapsulation and byte-stream reconstruction before the SAR reader can open the result; the reconstructed result is an ordinary SAR v1.0 archive. The approach can in principle address any byte-level loss including Global Header loss and CD/Footer loss, provided the external parity is sufficient. It does not change the fundamental design boundary that the RECOVERY TLV parity inside the CD is co-located with and subject to the same failure modes as the CD itself (COLD-002). The approach requires a separate container format or storage protocol specification; SAR v1.0 defines none. No new finding is required beyond COLD-001 and COLD-002; the approach is an implementation and deployment guidance item.

objectives.title: Tape-block and storage-layer parity approach evaluation
objectives.summary: Storage-layer parity (tape block ECC, RAID, sector-level redundancy) operates below the SAR layer. The original SAR byte stream is unchanged. A specification-compliant SAR reader can read the reconstructed byte stream directly; no SAR-level preprocessing is required. The recovered result is an ordinary SAR v1.0 archive. This approach can address any byte-level loss regardless of its position in the archive structure, including the Global Header leading fields (COLD-001) and the CD/Footer region (COLD-002). Section 9.2 defines the SAR-level precondition that unusable positions be known before RECOVERY decoding, and `plan_archive_repair()` accepts caller-supplied archive erasure ranges. Translation of storage-layer error information into those archive byte ranges is outside the reviewed SAR archive representation and recovery API contract. Recovery is unavailable when the caller or storage integration cannot produce usable erasure ranges. This bounded design risk is recorded in M13-SPEC-001.

objectives.title: Future profile-defined redundant manifest approach evaluation and finding classification
objectives.summary: An ordinary SAR Application Data Object could carry manifest or index bytes (such as a CD copy or offset array) using standard SAR entry framing (LFH and payload). SAR v1.0 does not currently define how such an entry is identified as a redundant manifest. A future profile would need to define its identification convention, placement, archive binding, freshness, duplicate handling, and conflict-resolution semantics if this design were adopted. No duplicate Global Header, Central Dictionary, end marker, or Footer is inherently required. Placement before the covered entries may improve physical survivability after terminal-anchor loss, but placement alone does not define interoperable discovery or authenticity. This remains an evaluated future profile design option rather than a resolved SAR v1.0 feature. The retained specification gap (SPEC-002) is limited to a SAR-specific external recovery sidecar and archive-binding mechanism; external container approaches remain separate deployment options evaluated in M13a.6-OBJ-06. findings.title: Unchecked `as u16` narrowing conversion in `global_header_flags_bytes`
findings.summary: `global_header_flags_bytes()` uses an unchecked `as u16` narrowing conversion for the flags size. Under default limits the cast is safe, but with non-default or unlimited limits the cast silently truncates, producing incorrect AEAD AAD bytes.
findings.current_behavior: `global_header_flags_bytes()` casts `header.flags_bytes.len()` (a usize) to u16 using `as u16` without a checked conversion. When `max_global_flags_bytes` is set above u16::MAX or `ResourceLimits::unlimited()` is in effect, the cast silently truncates, producing incorrect AAD bytes for AEAD computation.
findings.expected_behavior: The flags size must be encoded into the AAD bytes using a checked conversion that returns an error on overflow rather than silently truncating.
findings.impact: Silent truncation at AAD construction would cause AEAD authentication to fail for all encrypted entries when the flags buffer exceeds 65535 bytes, without a clear overflow error at the point of failure. Not exploitable under default limits.

evidence.description: `let flags_size = header.flags_bytes.len() as u16;` - unchecked narrowing conversion from usize to u16

evidence.locator: function `write_global_header()`, checked conversion of Global Flags byte length
evidence.description: `write_global_header` uses `u16::try_from(...)` for size encoding at the same location; the inconsistency is clear.

requirements: Use a checked conversion when encoding the Global Flags byte length into the u16 AAD field and return the appropriate existing error on overflow.

notes: Under default ResourceLimits, flags_bytes.len() <= 65535 == u16::MAX, so no truncation occurs in practice. The risk only materializes with non-default or unlimited limits.

Progress (WP-2a, M13b): the unchecked `as u16` conversion is eliminated by construction. Global Flags are a fixed four-byte field, so global_header_flags_bytes() and sar_crypto::aad::global_header_aad_bytes() write a constant Flags Size of 4 (the latter now takes &[u8; 4]); global_header_flags_bytes() returns Result and validates version and reserved bits. No variable flags buffer or flags-size limit remains, so the original overflow acceptance test is not applicable. crates/sar-crypto/src/aad.rs was also affected, although affected_artifacts lists only format.rs. Status is unchanged pending controller closure.

acceptance_criteria: Test that `global_header_flags_bytes` returns an error when flags buffer length exceeds u16::MAX under non-default limits.

findings.title: `audit()` data-area scan lacks entry-count limit check
findings.summary: `ArchiveReader::audit()` retains one `ArchiveAuditEntryReport` per scanned entry without enforcing the configured maximum entry count before retaining the report.

evidence.description: No `check_entry_count` call in the `audit()` loop body before `entries.push(...)`.
`limits.check_entry_count(file_count_usize)?;` is present in `parse_central_dictionary()` but not replicated in the data-area scan paths.

notes: `verify()` retains offsets rather than full audit reports, and `next_entry()` does not retain prior reports. This finding is limited to the retained-report behavior of `audit()`.

The minimum parseable LFH estimate in the audit record is 20 bytes with no optional fields, zero payload, and a zero-length name; the estimate is illustrative rather than a practical allocation forecast.

acceptance_criteria: Deterministic test verifying audit() returns LimitExceeded when entry count exceeds the configured limit. Use a small explicit limit (e.g., 2 allowed entries) and a valid archive containing more entries than the limit.

findings.current_behavior: The `audit()` data-area scan advances through parseable entries and pushes one `ArchiveAuditEntryReport` into its retained `entries` vector for each entry. The loop does not call `ResourceLimits::check_entry_count` before the push, so `max_entry_count` does not bound the number of retained reports. `verify()` retains offsets in a separate vector and `next_entry()` does not itself retain prior reports; those paths must not be conflated with the primary `audit()` allocation behavior.
findings.impact: For attacker-controlled archives, retained report memory and scan CPU can grow linearly with the number of parseable entries inside the permitted archive region rather than stopping at `max_entry_count`. The report vector has nontrivial inline storage per entry, and populated owned fields may add per-entry allocations. Archive size still provides an outer bound, but the default archive-size ceiling permits far more entries than the default entry-count limit and can cause memory exhaustion or prolonged processing before the scan ends.

requirements: Maintain a checked running entry count in `audit()` and enforce `max_entry_count` before retaining another `ArchiveAuditEntryReport`.
Return the existing limit-exceeded status without changing unrelated archive parsing or wire-format behavior.
constraints: Use a deterministic regression test with a deliberately small configured limit.

findings.title: TLV type IDs 0x05-0x0F accepted in violation of specification
findings.summary: The `classify_type()` function in tlv.rs leaves TLV type IDs 0x05..=0x0F to a wildcard accept arm. The specification explicitly reserves these IDs and requires a reserved-value error. The parser is fail-open for these IDs.
findings.current_behavior: `classify_type()` covers 0x00 (rejected), 0x01-0x04 (accepted), 0x10-0x1F (FEC dispatch), 0x20-0x2F (rejected), 0x30-0x3F (accepted), 0x40/0x41/0x4F (CDC accepted), 0x42-0x4E (rejected), 0x50-0xFF (rejected), and `_` wildcard (accepted). IDs 0x05..=0x0F fall to the wildcard and are parsed, accumulated, and returned without error.
findings.expected_behavior: Reserved TLV type IDs 0x05..=0x0F must be rejected with a reserved-value status before any accumulate or accept path. The dispatch must be exhaustive and fail closed for every possible input byte.
findings.impact: The parser accepts values that the specification designates as reserved and maps to a reserved-value error. This is a confirmed conformance and interoperability defect. No independent security bypass is demonstrated by the audit evidence, so severity is low while remediation priority remains high.

evidence.description: Explicit RESERVED designation for TLV type IDs 0x05-0x0F. The specification requires reserved values produce SAR_ERR_RESERVED_VALUE.
`classify_type()` wildcard arm accepts 0x05-0x0F without error; gap in explicit range coverage.

normative_basis.requirement: TLV type IDs 0x05-0x0F are RESERVED. Reserved values must produce SAR_ERR_RESERVED_VALUE.

requirements: Reject every reserved TLV type ID in 0x05..=0x0F with the specified reserved-value status before any accumulation or acceptance path.
Keep TLV type classification exhaustive and fail closed for every possible input byte.

acceptance_criteria: Test that each TLV type ID in 0x05..=0x0F is rejected with a reserved-value error by `parse_tlvs`.

notes: Reference (WP-2a, M13b): not addressed by WP-2a; TLV 0x05-0x0F reserved assignments remain owned by WP-2b.

Progress (WP-2b, M13b): classify_type() is now exhaustive over all 256 type IDs. 0x05-0x0F, 0x20, 0x2A-0x2F and 0x33-0x3F return SAR_ERR_RESERVED_VALUE on both parse_tlvs and write_tlvs; 0x21-0x29 return SAR_ERR_UNSUPPORTED; RECOVERY and CDC classification and duplicate-TLV handling are unchanged. crates/sar-core/tests/tlv_registry_tests.rs covers every identifier. Status is unchanged pending final diff review and controller closure.

findings.title: `GlobalFlags` undefined bits and extension bytes - normative behavior undefined
findings.summary: The specification does not explicitly define how SAR v1.0 readers must handle undefined bits in the first 32 Global Flags bits or nonzero extension bytes beyond the first four bytes. Current implementation behavior is recorded, but normative resolution is required before that behavior can be assessed or changed.
findings.current_behavior: Both `parse_global_header()` and `ArchiveReader::read_global_header()` call `GlobalFlags::from_bits_truncate()` to parse the 32-bit flags word, silently discarding bits 6, 7, 11-15, 21-23, and 31. Extension bytes beyond the first 4 bytes are stored but not semantically validated. `validate_global_flags()` does not reject unrecognized bits.
findings.normative_question: 1. Must undefined bits in the first 32-bit Global Flags word be zero? 2. Are additional Global Flags bytes an extensibility mechanism? 3. If additional bytes are allowed, how must unknown nonzero bits in those bytes be handled by a SAR v1.0 implementation? 4. Which SAR status applies when unsupported or reserved global-flag bits are encountered?

evidence.description: `GlobalFlags::from_bits_truncate(u32::from_le_bytes(low))` silently drops undefined bits.
`GlobalFlags::from_bits_truncate(u32::from_le_bytes(low))` - same pattern in reader path.

evidence.locator: function `validate_global_flags()`, undefined-bit and extension-byte validation rules
evidence.description: `validate_global_flags()` checks only specific flag combinations; does not reject unrecognized bits.
No explicit MUST-be-zero requirement for undefined bits in the 32-bit Global Flags word.

resolution.summary: Global Flags is a fixed four-byte field in SAR 1.0; all unassigned bits are reserved and MUST be zero; a nonzero reserved bit is rejected with SAR_ERR_RESERVED_VALUE.
resolution.rationale: Normative decision incorporated into specification.md (commit(s) cc65562). Normative resolution is distinct from implementation remediation, which is tracked by the linked M13b implementation_spec_mismatch findings and is not complete.

notes: Normative resolution: resolved. Implementation remediation: pending, tracked by M13-PARSER-017.

findings.title: TLS_EXPORTER KMS unsupported and mismatched parameters are not validated end-to-end
findings.summary: `parse_tls_exporter_kms_payload()` accepts any AEAD algorithm ID, any Global Header hash algorithm ID, and any nonzero `derived_key_length`. In-repo TLS_EXPORTER consumers preserve these values in `KmsContext` but do not validate them before operational key use, so unsupported or mismatched parameters are not guaranteed to fail closed as required.
findings.current_behavior: `parse_tls_exporter_kms_payload()` validates label/context/KDF-reserved/flags and only rejects zero `derived_key_length`. `aead_algo_id`, `global_header_hash_algo_id`, and nonzero `derived_key_length` are stored in `TlsExporterParams` and flow through `build_kms_context()`/`build_kms_context_for_additional_control()` into `KmsContext::TlsExporter` without in-repo registry or consistency checks. `resolve_cek()` then delegates TLS_EXPORTER handling to `external_key()` and does not validate those fields.
findings.expected_behavior: When TLS_EXPORTER KMS parameters are encountered, unsupported or reserved AEAD/hash IDs and derived-length/AEAD mismatches must be rejected on an end-to-end fail-closed path before operational key use or plaintext release, with status mapping consistent with SAR unsupported/reserved/invalid-length handling.
findings.impact: Unsupported AEAD/hash IDs can currently be accepted as operational KMS metadata without any guaranteed in-repo rejection. For mismatched derived lengths, rejection depends on external provider behavior: a provider that honors the mismatched length can fail later (for example `InvalidLength` at AEAD key-length checks, or `AuthFailed` on the additional-control path due to error mapping), while a provider that ignores the length can proceed without detecting the mismatch. No plaintext-release bypass was demonstrated.

evidence.locator: function `parse_tls_exporter_kms_payload()`, unsupported and reserved parameter validation
evidence.description: The parser records `aead_algo_id`, `global_header_hash_algo_id`, and nonzero `derived_key_length` without registry validation or AEAD/length consistency enforcement.

evidence.locator: functions `build_kms_context()` and `decode_ordinary_archive_entry_from_parts()`, TLS_EXPORTER context building and archive-entry AEAD decryption
evidence.description: TLS_EXPORTER payloads are parsed into `KmsParams::TlsExporter` and passed to `resolve_cek`; archive entry decrypt validates LFH `encr_algo_id` and key length at AEAD use but does not validate TLS_EXPORTER AEAD/hash IDs or derived-length consistency.

Additional control-stream TLS_EXPORTER context parsing feeds `KmsContext::TlsExporter` for CEK resolution; parser field validation failures are mapped to `AuthFailed`, but unsupported AEAD/hash IDs and nonzero mismatched lengths are not validated in this path.
`resolve_cek()` delegates TLS_EXPORTER material to `external_key()` and performs no AEAD/hash/derived-length validation for `KmsParams::TlsExporter`.
AEAD operations enforce 32-byte key length at key use, so provider-supplied non-32 keys fail at cryptographic use time rather than TLS_EXPORTER KMS parse time.

normative_basis.locator: Section 5.3.3, Mode 0x04 TLS_EXPORTER table (Derived Key Length)
normative_basis.requirement: Derived Key Length MUST match the selected AEAD algorithm requirements.

normative_basis.locator: Section 18.6.2 `TLS_EXPORTER KMS Requirements`, requirement `unsupported exporter, KDF, hash, AEAD, or KMS parameters MUST fail closed`
normative_basis.requirement: Unsupported exporter, KDF, hash, AEAD, or KMS parameters MUST fail closed.

normative_basis.locator: Section 18.6.3 `Exporter Label and Context`, `Global Header Hash Algo ID` fail-closed requirement
normative_basis.requirement: Unsupported or reserved Global Header hash and unsupported AEAD/context/KDF values MUST fail closed.

acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate that unsupported/reserved TLS_EXPORTER AEAD and Global Header hash IDs are rejected on a deterministic in-repo end-to-end consumer path.
Demonstrate that TLS_EXPORTER derived-length/AEAD mismatches are rejected before operational cryptographic use on in-repo consumer paths.
Verify fail-closed status mapping for malformed/reserved/unsupported/invalid-length TLS_EXPORTER parameter failures remains explicit and stable.

resolution.summary: TLS_EXPORTER KMS payloads are parsed with the canonical parse_tls_exporter_kms_payload when an archive Global Header is read and on header receipt in the non-TCP transport path; malformed, reserved and unsupported combinations fail closed with the canonical status mapping.
resolution.rationale: The current specification (Section 5.3.3) defines the TLS_EXPORTER payload without an AEAD ID and with a fixed 32-byte derived length, so the AEAD-ID and derived-length/AEAD-mismatch requirements are superseded; the Entry Encr Algo ID is validated per LFH. Hash ID (reserved vs unsupported SHA3-256), version, KDF, derived length, label and salt validation now run at the archive-header boundary and on transport header receipt, with deterministic negative tests. Directional TLS_EXPORTER session bootstrap, exporter acquisition and the TCP binding remain M13b.4 and are not part of this finding's requirements.

notes: Closure (SAR-M13b-WP7C-IMPLEMENTATION-001): The current specification (Section 5.3.3) defines the TLS_EXPORTER payload without an AEAD ID and with a fixed 32-byte derived length, so the AEAD-ID and derived-length/AEAD-mismatch requirements are superseded; the Entry Encr Algo ID is validated per LFH. Hash ID (reserved vs unsupported SHA3-256), version, KDF, derived length, label and salt validation now run at the archive-header boundary and on transport header receipt, with deterministic negative tests. Directional TLS_EXPORTER session bootstrap, exporter acquisition and the TCP binding remain M13b.4 and are not part of this finding's requirements.

findings.title: CLI password input warnings and guidance do not clearly steer operators away from argv/environment exposure
findings.summary: CLI password input surfaces expose `--password` and `SAR_PASSWORD` without concise warning text, and the README encryption example demonstrates `--password` usage without warning or safer-path guidance.
findings.current_behavior: `load_password()` precedence is explicit CLI `--password`, then `SAR_PASSWORD`, then interactive prompt. The `Create`, `Extract`, and `Verify` argument definitions expose `--password` without warning/help text, and the README encryption example uses `--password` directly with no exposure warning or interactive-prompt recommendation.
findings.expected_behavior: CLI-facing help metadata and documentation examples should include concise warnings about argv/environment exposure and recommend safer interactive or managed-secret input paths, while documenting password-source precedence.
findings.impact: Operators can reasonably treat argv/environment password input as standard usage because these channels are exposed without concise warning text at the option surface and in repository examples. This is a documentation/usability secret-handling risk, not a demonstrated cryptographic bypass.

evidence.description: The `Create`, `Extract`, and `Verify` CLI subcommands each expose `#[arg(long)] password: Option<String>` with no warning/help text attached to those argument declarations.

evidence.locator: function `load_password()`, explicit argument then `SAR_PASSWORD` environment variable then prompt precedence
evidence.description: `PASSWORD_ENV` is defined as `SAR_PASSWORD`, and `load_password()` prefers the explicit CLI value and then the inherited environment variable before prompting.
The encryption example uses `--password "test-password"` for both `sar create` and `sar extract` without warning text or guidance that interactive prompting is the safer default.

notes: The interactive prompt path already satisfies the requirement for a non-argv/non-environment password channel.
Risk and warning scope is platform- and tooling-dependent; this finding does not claim identical argv/environment exposure semantics everywhere.

Closure (SAR-M13b-WP7C-IMPLEMENTATION-001): Help for create/extract/verify and the README encryption example no longer present --password as the default path; warnings distinguish argv/process-listing exposure, shell history, and environment inheritance/telemetry without claiming identical platform behavior. Tests pin the help text and the existing precedence. Noninteractive automation keeps working via --password or SAR_PASSWORD; no managed-secret-file option exists and none was added.

acceptance_criteria: CLI-facing documentation and help surfaces explicitly describe password-source precedence and safer recommended usage.
Encrypted-workflow examples no longer imply argv or inherited environment input is the default recommended path.
Warnings distinguish argv exposure, shell history risk, and environment inheritance/telemetry risk without asserting identical behavior across all platforms.

findings.title: Secret containers and authentication-failure buffers are zeroized in audited crypto paths
findings.summary: The audited crypto code consistently wraps passwords, CEKs, and derived keys in zeroizing containers, and the AEAD decrypt paths explicitly clear plaintext work buffers before returning authentication failures.

evidence.description: `SecretBytes` and `SecretString` are defined as `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` and `Zeroizing<String>`.

evidence.locator: function `aead_decrypt()`, auth-failure branches that zeroize temporary plaintext buffers
evidence.description: Both AEAD decrypt branches call `buf.zeroize()` before returning `AuthFailed` on tag verification failure.
PBKDF2 derives the CEK into a `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` buffer and returns it as `SecretBytes`.
Argon2 derives the CEK into a `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` buffer and returns it as `SecretBytes`.

notes: This observation is limited to practical zeroization within Rust-managed memory and audited call paths; it does not claim guaranteed physical media erasure.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.2: the audited crypto code uses zeroizing containers for passwords, CEKs, and derived keys, and explicitly clears plaintext work buffers before returning authentication failures.

findings.title: Authentication and AEAD tag failures are handled as hard fail-closed errors before downstream processing
findings.summary: The audited archive and transport paths authenticate and decrypt before decompression or session processing, reject post-binding plaintext in TLS_EXPORTER sessions, and propagate tag or key mismatches as hard authentication failures without exposing plaintext.

evidence.description: `decode_payload_v2()` authenticates and decrypts first and only then calls `decode_payload()` for decompression.
TLS_EXPORTER-bound streams reject unencrypted post-binding entries and map additional-control-stream AEAD failures to `SarError::AuthFailed` before forwarding any plaintext.
`auth_failure_happens_before_decompression()` verifies corrupted ciphertext returns `SarError::AuthFailed` before decompression.
`aead_failure_does_not_expose_plaintext()` verifies wrong AAD returns `AuthFailed` and never returns plaintext.
Post-binding plaintext on both primary and additional QUIC control streams is rejected with authentication failure semantics.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.2: archive and transport call paths treat authentication and AEAD tag failures as hard errors before decompression, session processing, or plaintext release.

findings.title: Secret-dependent comparisons are limited and use constant-time or library-internal verification paths
findings.summary: The audited scope does not open-code AEAD tag comparisons, and its explicit digest comparison helper uses `subtle::ConstantTimeEq` after a public length check. No additional meaningfully timing-sensitive secret comparison requiring bespoke handling was identified in the reviewed cryptographic paths.

evidence.description: `ct_eq()` returns early only on length mismatch and otherwise delegates digest equality to `subtle::ConstantTimeEq`.
AEAD tag verification stays inside `decrypt_inout_detached()` from the crypto libraries rather than using a handwritten byte-by-byte comparison.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.2: the audited cryptographic paths either use a constant-time digest helper or rely on crypto-library tag verification, and no additional meaningfully timing-sensitive secret comparison requiring bespoke handling was identified.

findings.title: Cryptographic dependency selection is narrow and unsupported non-AEAD modes fail closed at dispatch
findings.summary: The audited workspace and `sar-crypto` crate use a focused set of high-level crypto dependencies for supported SAR functionality, and algorithm dispatch rejects unsupported or non-AEAD encryption modes instead of silently downgrading to weaker behavior.

evidence.description: Workspace crypto dependencies are limited to AES-GCM, XChaCha20-Poly1305, SHA-2, BLAKE3, PBKDF2, Argon2, zeroize, subtle, rand_core/getrandom, and HMAC.
`sar-crypto` consumes the workspace crypto crates directly and does not enable extra algorithm families beyond the audited SAR surface.

evidence.locator: functions `aead_encrypt()` and `aead_decrypt()`, algorithm dispatch and unsupported branch
evidence.description: Supported AEAD operations are implemented through the libraries' high-level `KeyInit` and `encrypt_inout_detached`/`decrypt_inout_detached` APIs.
`validate_encr_algo_id()` accepts only plaintext, AES-256-GCM, and XChaCha20-Poly1305; unsupported or reserved encryption IDs fail closed.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.2: the audited SAR crypto surface uses a narrow dependency set and fail-closed algorithm dispatch rather than silently enabling unsupported non-AEAD modes.

findings.title: Extractor does not enforce canonicalized, directory-relative confinement for final filesystem mutations
findings.summary: The CLI extractor lexically validates archive names and checks existing parent components with `symlink_metadata()`, but it never canonicalizes the selected output root or final target before write, rename, chmod, chown, or timestamp operations. Because those final mutations use ordinary path-based filesystem calls, a pre-existing output-root symlink or a concurrent path-replacement race can redirect extraction effects outside the intended root.
findings.current_behavior: Current (M13b.3 Packages A-F, branch m13b3-extraction-platform-evidence): the original path-based Unix mutation model (the `create_dir_all()`/`symlink_metadata()` walk followed by path-based create, rename, remove, chmod, chown and timestamp calls) has been replaced by directory-descriptor-relative operations. On Unix targets `ExtractionRoot` (crates/sar-cli/src/extraction/root_unix.rs) opens the selected root once as a directory descriptor (a root symlink is resolved exactly once) and performs every directory walk, mkdir, staging-file creation, rename, symlink creation, unlink and metadata mutation relative to descriptors (openat, mkdirat, renameat, unlinkat, symlinkat, fchown, futimens, fchmod) with O_NOFOLLOW directory traversal and O_EXCL staging files. Escapes and unconfinable paths report SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE (Package B), distinct logical paths reaching one destination object report SAR_ERR_PATH_COLLISION (Package C), the Section 6.1.5 final state is implemented without deleting pre-existing content (Package D), and run-owned temporary artifacts are tracked and cleaned by identity with partial-result and cleanup diagnostics (Package E). On targets without `cfg(unix)` the remaining path-based extractor was removed (Package F): `sar extract` refuses before the archive is opened or the destination is touched, with SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE, because confinement cannot be established; create, list, inspect, verify and repair are unaffected. Residuals: the Unix backend is runtime-tested on Linux, and FreeBSD 15.1 only for the Package A backend; macOS runtime is unverified; case-folding and Unicode-normalizing destination tests have not run on the development hosts; POSIX provides no atomic identity-checked unlink or rename, so a hostile writer to the destination retains a narrow check/use window for run-owned temporary names; extraction is neither all-or-nothing nor crash-recoverable; Windows and other non-Unix targets have no secure extraction backend.
findings.expected_behavior: Before each filesystem mutation, extraction should resolve and confine the effective target beneath the selected extraction root using symlink-safe canonicalization and/or directory-relative operations so that later path replacement cannot redirect writes or metadata restoration outside the permitted tree.
findings.impact: An attacker who can influence pre-existing filesystem state for the chosen extraction destination, or who can concurrently replace path components inside an attacker-writable extraction tree, can redirect file creation, atomic rename, symlink creation, or post-write metadata restoration outside the intended root. If extraction is run with `--preserve-owner`, successful exploitation can also redirect privileged ownership changes to an attacker-chosen target path.

evidence.locator: function `extract_archive()`, extraction orchestration and final `finalize_directory_metadata(...)` call
evidence.description: Historical (M13a.4 audit baseline, reviewed commit 71e35d8; the cited path-based functions were replaced by descriptor-relative operations in M13b.3 Packages A-E): `extract_archive()` accepts the caller-supplied `output_dir`, calls `create_dir_all()`, then performs reconstructed-file writes and final directory metadata application through raw `PathBuf` values without canonicalizing the extraction root.

Historical (M13a.4 audit baseline, reviewed commit 71e35d8; the cited path-based functions were replaced by descriptor-relative operations in M13b.3 Packages A-E): `prepare_output_file_path()` and `ensure_parent_directory_path()` join unchecked `output_dir` prefixes with lexical archive components, inspect parents with `symlink_metadata()`, and create directories with `create_dir()`/`set_permissions()`, but never prove the final resolved path remains beneath a canonical root.

Historical (M13a.4 audit baseline, reviewed commit 71e35d8; the cited path-based functions were replaced by descriptor-relative operations in M13b.3 Packages A-E): Temporary output paths are derived from the final `Path`, opened with `create_new`, and published with `rename()` using ordinary path resolution; no directory handle or post-resolution confinement check is retained across the check/use window.

Historical (M13a.4 audit baseline, reviewed commit 71e35d8; the cited path-based functions were replaced by descriptor-relative operations in M13b.3 Packages A-E): File and directory metadata restoration re-checks paths with `symlink_metadata()` but then calls `chown`, `set_file_times`, and `set_permissions` by path, so later replacement can change which inode receives the mutation.

evidence.locator: Section 22.4 `Path Security`, canonicalization and extraction-root confinement requirements
evidence.description: Historical wording from the M13a.4 baseline, superseded by the M13a.7 revision of Section 22.4 (see the current normative_basis entry): Before any write operation, target paths MUST be canonicalized, all symbolic links and segments MUST be resolved, and extraction MUST ensure the final path resides within the intended extraction root.

Current Unix backend: root opened once as a directory descriptor; all mutations use descriptor-relative *at calls with O_NOFOLLOW traversal and O_EXCL staging; metadata is applied to open descriptors.

Deterministic hook-injected race tests cover root-symlink resolution, parent replacement between check and mutation, symlink creation and data publication, and file/directory/owner metadata restoration. Run on Linux; Package A backend tests also ran on FreeBSD 15.1.

evidence.locator: tests `extraction_into_symlinked_root_resolves_it_once_and_leaves_no_staging_files` and the confined-symlink and permission tests
evidence.description: CLI-level evidence that extraction into a pre-existing symlinked root is confined and that compliant in-root content and metadata are still restored.
Non-Unix targets compile an uninhabited ExtractionRoot whose `open` always fails with SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE before any filesystem access; no path-based extractor remains.

Compiled only for non-Unix targets (type-checked for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu; never executed on a native non-Unix host). The refusal logic itself is unit-tested on Linux in policy.rs and the stub was exercised on Linux by temporarily selecting it, which is not native evidence.

normative_basis.locator: Section 22.4 `Path Security`, canonicalization and extraction-root confinement requirements
normative_basis.requirement: Historical wording from the M13a.4 baseline, superseded by the M13a.7 revision of Section 22.4: Before any write operation, target paths MUST be canonicalized. Implementations MUST resolve all symbolic links and segments to ensure the final path resides within the intended extraction root. If canonicalization fails or points outside the allowed scope, the implementation MUST return `SAR_ERR_IO` and MUST NOT attempt to create the file.

Every filesystem mutation during materialization MUST remain within the selected scope; lexical validation alone is insufficient; if an Entry destination escapes the scope or confinement cannot be established the implementation MUST return `SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE` and MUST NOT perform the affected mutation; later operations MUST NOT follow a materialized or pre-existing symbolic link outside the scope; distinct Full Logical Entry Paths mapping to one destination object MUST return `SAR_ERR_PATH_COLLISION`.

requirements: Constrain every extraction write, replacement, symlink creation, and metadata-restoration operation to a canonicalized extraction root so that pre-existing symlinks and later path replacement cannot redirect effects outside the permitted tree.

Eliminate the identified check/use windows in the extraction path, including temporary-file publication and post-write metadata restoration, or otherwise make those operations resolve against stable directory-relative state.

Add deterministic hostile-filesystem tests covering pre-existing output-root symlinks or equivalent confined-root setup and path-replacement attempts against both data writes and metadata restoration paths.

Targets without a secure extraction backend must refuse extraction with SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE before any mutation instead of using a path-based fallback; a future Windows backend requires a separately scoped secure implementation and native validation.

notes: Historical baseline (M13a.4, commit 71e35d8), preserved: the superseded `current_behavior` read: `extract_archive()` creates `output_dir` with `create_dir_all()` and then passes the raw path through `prepare_output_file_path()` and `ensure_parent_directory_path()`. Those helpers walk components with `symlink_metadata()` and `create_dir()` checks, but `write_bytes_via_temp()`, `write_sparse_payload_via_temp()`, `finalize_temp_file()`, `extract_symlink_entry()`, `apply_file_metadata()`, and `finalize_directory_metadata()` all perform their final create, rename, remove, chmod, chown, or timestamp operations through ordinary path-based APIs without canonicalizing the resolved target or holding directory-relative handles across the check/use boundary.

Progress (M13b.3 Package A, SAR-M13b3-EXTRACTION-WPA-IMPLEMENTATION-001): on Unix targets the extraction root is opened once as a directory descriptor (a root symlink is resolved exactly once) and every directory walk, directory creation, temporary-file creation, rename, symlink creation, unlink and metadata mutation is performed relative to descriptors via openat/mkdirat/renameat/unlinkat/symlinkat/fchown/futimens/fchmod, with O_NOFOLLOW directory traversal and O_EXCL temporary files named independently of the archived basename. Regular-file metadata is applied to the open staging file before publication; staging files are always created 0600 and, when no permission restoration applies, receive the default creat(0666) mode (umask and default ACLs honored, learned from an empty probe file, no process umask change) via fchmod just before the rename; directories are created 0700 and never exposed with permissive modes. Deterministic race-injection tests (root_unix.rs) cover parent replacement between check and mutation, symlinked-root substitution, staging publication, symlink creation and directory metadata. Status intentionally left confirmed: Windows and other non-Unix targets use an unhardened path-based fallback (Package F), macOS runtime validation is outstanding (Linux and FreeBSD 15.1 sar-cli tests pass), and path-status mapping, collisions, replacement semantics and partial-extraction cleanup remain in Packages B-E.

Progress (M13b.3 Package B, SAR-M13b3-EXTRACTION-WPB-IMPLEMENTATION-001): materialization escapes, unconfinable paths and refusal to traverse existing symlinks now report SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE (701); malformed archive metadata (empty/NUL paths, NUL symlink payloads) stays SAR_ERR_MALFORMED and I/O errors are not remapped. Symlink targets are evaluated lexically from the link directory without filesystem lookups (sub/../ok and . accepted, dangling accepted, escaping or absolute/backslash/drive targets rejected) and the stored target is created verbatim. Status intentionally left confirmed: collisions (Package C), replacement semantics (D), cleanup (E) and non-Unix posture (F) remain open.

Progress (M13b.3 Package C, SAR-M13b3-EXTRACTION-WPC-IMPLEMENTATION-001): extraction keeps a bounded per-run ledger that maps each exactly spelled SAR logical path (component tree) to the destination object it reached, identified by the host filesystem itself (device and inode from fstat/fstatat without following symlinks; no name folding or normalization is performed by SAR). Directory components, staged files and symlinks are claimed; a differently spelled logical path reaching an object already claimed by another path (case folding, Unicode normalization, aliases, hard links) fails with SAR_ERR_PATH_COLLISION (700) before the staging object is created and is re-checked immediately before publication. Repeating the identical logical path is not a collision, replaces its previous claim and keeps the current last-wins behavior; unclaimed pre-existing objects never count as evidence. Ledger bookkeeping is charged against max_total_pipeline_memory. The ledger is individually bounded by `max_total_pipeline_memory`; it is not an aggregate accounting of all archive-reader and CLI allocations. Capacity is reserved before the publication rename, released if the rename fails, and committed afterwards without a fresh limit check, so a resource-limit failure never follows a successful publication; replacing a prior claim for the same logical path needs no extra capacity. Filesystem-dependent cases are capability-probed in tests (case-insensitive and normalizing destinations skip on case-sensitive hosts; SAR_TEST_FS_PROBE_DIR can select such a destination) and aliasing is also simulated deterministically with hard links. The non-Unix fallback identifies objects by canonical path and is best effort and untested at runtime (Package F). Status intentionally left confirmed: replacement semantics (D), cleanup (E) and non-Unix posture (F) remain open.

Progress (M13b.3 Package E, SAR-M13b3-EXTRACTION-WPE-IMPLEMENTATION-001): ordinary Unix extraction remains fail-fast and non-transactional, and a failure after destination changes never reports success and states that partial destination changes may remain. Run-owned temporary objects (staging files, staging symlinks, probe files and moved-aside directories) are registered in a bounded per-run record together with a parent directory descriptor and the object identity captured at creation; cleanup acts only on registered artifacts, only through that descriptor, and only while the name still reaches the recorded identity, so a substituted symlink or unrecognized object is left in place and reported rather than followed or deleted, and the extraction root is never scanned for `.sar-tmp-*` names. A failed directory replacement restores the moved-aside directory when the original name is free and records a failed restoration; after a successful replacement publication the published object is kept, recognized run-created content of the moved-aside subtree is removed, and unrecognized content is retained and returned as an error. The primary SAR status is preserved and the CLI reports cleanup failures separately, without extracted content, with a nonzero exit status. Process crashes and abrupt termination can still leave staging files, moved-aside directories and partial extraction results; no crash-recovery journal exists. The finding is not closed: platform support (Package F) and the final audit disposition remain open.

Package D (SAR-M13b3-EXTRACTION-WPD-IMPLEMENTATION-001) record added by Package F: the final logical state of Section 6.1.5 is implemented on Unix (last complete Entry wins; a non-directory Entry replaces an earlier directory and its earlier descendants; a later descendant turns an earlier file or symlink into an implicit directory; the last explicit directory Entry determines directory metadata). Only objects created by the current run are ever removed, proven by identities recorded in the collision ledger; pre-existing directories and unrecognized content are never deleted and fail with SAR_ERR_ALREADY_EXISTS, and removal depth is bounded (64 levels, SAR_ERR_LIMIT_EXCEEDED).

Progress (M13b.3 Package F, SAR-M13b3-EXTRACTION-WPF-IMPLEMENTATION-001): platform posture and evidence reconciliation. (1) The non-Unix path-based extractor (`root_fallback.rs`) is removed: it no longer compiled (the Package C collision ledger API was not updated for it, so the non-Unix build was already broken at the baseline) and could never satisfy Section 22.4 (no reserved-name, alternate-data-stream or reparse-point handling, best-effort canonical-path identity, no descriptor confinement). On targets without cfg(unix) extraction is refused with SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE before the archive is opened or the destination is touched; the former non-Unix canonical-path identity, filetime path metadata and the non-Unix `filetime` dependency are removed. Compatibility: regular-file and directory extraction, previously nominally available on non-Unix hosts, is now refused (the previous code did not build, so no working non-Unix extraction was lost). (2) Platform matrix: Linux implemented and runtime-tested; FreeBSD 15.1 runtime-tested for the Package A backend only (later packages were not natively re-run there); macOS intended Unix backend, native runtime unverified; Windows and other non-Unix not implemented and refused. (3) Candidate disposition (planning candidates C-1..C-11): C-1 resolved (Package B, SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE); C-2 resolved (Package B, lexical symlink-target evaluation, targets never rewritten; the residual that a lexically accepted target such as `x -> s1/..` may resolve outside the scope after extraction through a later-created link affects consumers, not the extractor, which never traverses links); C-3 resolved on Unix by filesystem identity (Package C), case-folding and Unicode-normalizing destination tests are capability-probed and skipped on the development host, hard-link aliasing is simulated deterministically; C-4 resolved on Unix (Package D); C-5 resolved (Package A, short random staging names, maximum-length basename test); C-6 resolved on Unix (Package A, metadata applied to open descriptors before publication, directories created 0700); C-7 resolved on Unix as a contract, not as transactional behavior (Package E; no all-or-nothing guarantee, no persistent crash-recovery journal); C-8 resolved (documentation updated in Package F); C-9 resolved (EXTRACT-002..006 annotated, historical text preserved); C-10 recorded, not implemented (see M13-EXTRACT-008); C-11 recorded as M13-EXTRACT-007, not fixed. (4) Not closed: acceptance criteria 1 and 2 are demonstrated on Linux (and for the Package A backend on FreeBSD 15.1) and criterion 3 is covered by the existing CLI roundtrip and metadata tests, but macOS runtime is unverified, case-folding/normalizing filesystem tests were not executed, Windows has no secure backend, and POSIX check/use windows remain where atomic identity operations are unavailable. Recommendation: keep status confirmed until the Controller accepts these platform limitations; then resolve with an explicit accepted-limitations record. Not pulled into Package F: `repair` temporary output (M13-EXTRACT-007), archive-reader Name/Path validation, HIDDEN_ATTR/FORCE_SYNC/OP_CODE (M13-EXTRACT-008), cross-Partition extraction (M13-BOUNDARY-003) and M13b.4 stream/session materialization. Test gating (final review, SAR-M13b3-EXTRACTION-WPF-FINAL-REVIEW-001): integration tests that perform a successful or extraction-dependent CLI extract are `#[cfg(unix)]` per test (whole-file for cli_fragment_group_tests), so a native non-Unix run does not report intentional refusal as a failure; non-extraction tests remain on all platforms and crates/sar-cli/tests/cli_platform_guard_tests.rs (`#![cfg(not(unix))]`) asserts SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE with no destination created. These guard tests and the non-Unix build are type-checked only via cross-compilation (x86_64-pc-windows-gnu) and have not run on a native non-Unix host.

acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate that regular-file, sparse-file, and symlink extraction refuse or correctly confine destinations when the selected extraction root itself resolves through a pre-existing symlink on the host filesystem; note that symlink parent components within the extraction tree are already rejected by existing path-walking checks (verified in M13-EXTRACT-002) and do not represent the unprotected scenario targeted by this criterion.
Demonstrate that path-replacement attempts cannot redirect temporary-file publication or post-write metadata restoration outside the extraction root.
Verify that successful extraction still restores in-root content and metadata for compliant archive names after the confinement hardening.

Document the security-support matrix (Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, Windows/non-Unix) without claiming validation beyond the executed evidence, and refuse extraction on targets without a secure backend before any mutation.

findings.title: Archive path parsing rejects common traversal and ambiguous host-path forms before joining
findings.summary: Archive extraction performs explicit lexical validation before joining names to the output tree. Empty names, absolute paths, UNC and verbatim prefixes, backslashes, NUL bytes, empty components, `.` components, `..` traversal, and Windows drive-prefixed components are rejected, and extraction refuses to walk through an existing symlink parent component.

evidence.locator: functions `validate_relative_archive_path()` and `ensure_parent_directory_path()`, traversal and symlink-parent rejection
evidence.description: `validate_relative_archive_path()` rejects absolute, UNC, drive-prefixed, backslash, NUL, empty, `.` and `..` forms, and `ensure_parent_directory_path()` refuses existing symlink parents.
CLI tests cover rejection of `../`, absolute, drive-prefixed, and UNC archive names and rejection of an existing symlink parent component during extraction.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.4: lexical archive-path validation rejects common traversal and ambiguous host-path forms before extraction joins names to the output tree, and existing symlink parents are refused.

notes: Package F reconciliation (M13b.3): historical evidence preserved. Path-syntax classification is now implemented by `SafeRelativePath` and the Full Logical Entry Path composition in crates/sar-cli/src/extraction/paths.rs; traversal, absolute, drive-prefixed, UNC and unconfinable paths report SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE (701) instead of the SAR_ERR_MALFORMED (100) recorded when this observation was verified, while empty or `.` components, an empty Name String and a separator-bearing Name String remain SAR_ERR_MALFORMED. The test names cited above may have been reworded or moved (for example crates/sar-cli/tests/cli_full_logical_path_tests.rs `invalid_path_string_components_are_rejected`, cli_metadata_tests.rs `hostile_paths_are_rejected`). Existing symlink parent components are still refused, now through descriptor-relative O_NOFOLLOW traversal (SAR_ERR_PATH_ESCAPE). findings.title: Staging chmod to 0o700 precedes child extraction; directory metadata finalization is deferred and occurs in reverse-depth order
findings.summary: On Unix, `create_restrictive_directory()` calls `fs::create_dir()` (which applies the process umask, typically yielding mode 0o755 with the standard umask of 0o022) and then calls `fs::set_permissions(path, 0o700)` as a separate step. Content extraction for a directory proceeds only after the `set_permissions` call succeeds; if it fails, extraction halts. Pending directory metadata is applied only after child extraction completes and in reverse-depth order, regular-file metadata is applied after temp-file publication, symlink metadata application is skipped, and restored modes are masked to ordinary permission bits so setuid, setgid, and sticky bits are not reintroduced.

evidence.description: `create_restrictive_directory()` calls `fs::create_dir(path)` to create the directory and then calls `fs::set_permissions(path, Permissions::from_mode(0o700))` on Unix. `fs::create_dir` passes mode 0o777 to the `mkdir` syscall, which applies the process umask; with the standard umask of 0o022 the effective creation mode is 0o755. The chmod is a separate step and not atomic with creation. Content extraction proceeds only after `set_permissions` returns `Ok(())`; if it returns an error, extraction halts.

`apply_file_metadata()` runs only after file publication, skips symlink paths, `finalize_directory_metadata()` applies directory metadata after child extraction in reverse depth order, and `apply_permissions()` masks restored modes with `0o0777`.
CLI tests verify directory permissions are applied after extraction and that restoring `0o4755` results in `0o755` on disk.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.4: content extraction for a directory proceeds only after `set_permissions(0o700)` succeeds (failing closed on error), final directory metadata is deferred until children are extracted in reverse-depth order, symlink metadata application is skipped, and special mode bits are stripped from restored permissions. Directory staging uses a create-then-chmod sequence; the initial creation mode is umask-determined (typically 0o755), but the directory is empty and unwritable by other principals during that window, and extraction content is written only after the chmod to 0o700 succeeds.

notes: Package F reconciliation (M13b.3): historical evidence preserved. The create-then-chmod race window noted above no longer exists on Unix: directories are created 0700 (never group- or world-accessible), regular-file metadata is applied to the open staging descriptor before atomic publication, and directory metadata is finalized through descriptors after all children in reverse-depth order. Restored modes are still masked to ordinary permission bits and setuid/setgid/sticky restoration remains disabled. Applies to Unix targets only; extraction is refused elsewhere.

findings.title: Current extractor exposes no hardlink creation path
findings.summary: The current entry model and CLI extractor handle only regular files, directories, symlinks, and empty areas. No archive entry kind or extraction branch creates hardlinks, so hardlink hazards are absent from the present extraction implementation rather than silently accepted.

evidence.description: `EntryKind` contains `RegularFile`, `Directory`, `Symlink`, and `EmptyArea` only; there is no hardlink entry kind.

evidence.locator: function `extract_non_fragment_entry()`, entry-kind dispatch without hardlink branch
evidence.description: `extract_non_fragment_entry()` matches only directory, symlink, regular-file, and empty-area cases; no hardlink creation path exists.

resolution.summary: Verified during M13a.4: the current SAR CLI extraction surface has no hardlink entry model or hardlink creation branch.

notes: Package F reconciliation (M13b.3): still accurate. The specification defines no hardlink Entry kind and the extractor creates no hardlinks; replacing a pre-existing hard-linked name by rename does not modify the other link, and hard-link aliasing of run-created objects is treated as a path collision or as not run-owned (never removed) by Packages C and D.

findings.title: Symlink target conformance and extraction-safety requirements are not normatively resolved
findings.summary: The specification defines a symlink entry as payload bytes passed to the host symlink-creation utility, but it does not state whether absolute, parent-traversing, or otherwise escaping symlink targets are conforming archive content, whether compliant extractors must preserve such targets verbatim, or whether they must reject them for extraction safety. The current CLI extractor rejects those targets by applying the same relative-path policy used for archive entry names.
findings.current_behavior: `extract_symlink_entry()` requires `--allow-symlinks`, retrieves `entry.metadata.symlink_target`, and then calls `validate_relative_archive_path(target)` before creating the link. That rejects absolute paths, parent traversal, empty components, UNC prefixes, drive prefixes, backslashes, and dot segments for symlink targets as well as entry names.
findings.normative_question: For SAR v1.0 symlink entries, are absolute or parent-traversing payload targets conforming archive content that a compliant extractor should preserve verbatim, or must compliant extractors reject or rewrite such targets to preserve extraction-root confinement? How does Section 22.4 Path Security apply to symlink target payloads versus the created link pathname?

evidence.locator: Section 15.3 Definition of a symlink file
evidence.description: The specification says symlink payload data is the target path string and MUST be passed to the host symlink creation utility, but it does not constrain whether the target may be absolute or escaping.
